The alphabet used by the [[Old Tongue]] is provided in [[The Wheel of Time Companion]].{{ref|{{twotc}}, Old Tongue|comp}} It first appeared, however, in the bonus content for the 2010 graphic novel of [[New Spring]].

==General Notes==
[[File:OT enhanced res.png|thumb|350px|The Old Tongue script as presented in the Wheel of Time Companion]]The Old Tongue on the Horn of Valere is described as "flowing" and that on Mat's dagger as "cursive", which implies that the letters may be written joined up rather than individually, or at least that it ''can'' be written like that.{{ref/book|2|2}}{{ref/book|5|3}} For ease of reading, use of the Old Tongue in the fandom on tattoos, inscriptions and other uses, including the [[The Wheel of Time (TV series)|TV series]], does not do this.

Variations in letter forms, what we might call typefaces or fonts, do exist. When Elayne accesses the [[Bearded man|library ter'angreal]] she notes that "some of the letters were shaped a little oddly, but the words were quite clear."{{ref/book|11|15}}
==The Alphabet (Letter Forms)==
There are thirty-seven letters on the Old Tongue and ten numerical symbols. The Companion does not call it an alphabet, but rather "letter forms"{{ref|{{twotc}}, Old Tongue|comp}} Compared to many languages that use an alphabet, this is a high number. English, of course, has 26 while Russian has 33. The Hungarian alphabet has 44, although many of these are modifications of the standard Roman alphabet (e.g. e with diacritical additions) as opposed to visually more distinct symbols. Brahmic-based scripts including Thai, Hindi and Bengali have between 43 and 50 letters. These seem a little closer to the Old Tongue, particularly Thai whose letters contain the same loop features (called heads).

Several of the letters in the Old Tongue resemble musical notes or notation. B (base clef), H and Z and 0 (musical notes).

Only one letter consists of two disconnected components: V.
===Vowels===
The Old Tongue has eleven vowel sounds plus the semivowel y. Six of these are bigrams in English, but it would be fair to assume that they represent a standardised vowel pronunciation.<gallery widths=150px heights=150px perrow=6>

===Consonants===
The Old Tongue has twenty-five consonant letters, including five which are bigraphs (DH, GH, ST, SH, TH). Similarly, we can assume that these form a standardised pronounciation.

==Phonetic Relationships==
The following relationships can be observed between the form of the letters and how they are pronounced:
*OU and OO have a similar form and sound.
*IE is a reflection of the OO/OU forms. It is formed by a widening the mouth, whereas OO is the opposite.
*V and W have a similar form
*SH and TH are similar in form and are both XXX sounds
*S and ST share the same 9-shaped form
*DH is written as the English G and is pronounced as a soft G as in Georgia.
==Relationships in Form==
The following show some similarity in how they are written with no apparent relationship in sound:
*D, T and U are all similar to the English N.
*The symbol of F looks very similar to the call sign of Zorro. Zorro means Fox in Spanish.
==Capitalisation==
We are told that capitalisation of words in the Old Tongue changes the meaning, often to stress importance or a larger scope than without.{{ref||comp}} The word aiel, for example, means dedicated, whereas Aiel with a capital means "stronger than that; it implies an oath written into your bones."{{ref/book|4|23}} It also appears in proper nouns e.g. Atha'an Miere.

While we know this exists, we don't know how it was implemented as we have not been handed upper case (majuscule) letter forms. One option is just to make the letters slightly larger, but this could be difficult in the case of AI, EI and other cases. Another option would be to add a marker like an underline or a dot above the letter.

==General Punctuation==
[[File:Thai script.jpg|thumb|250px|right|Thai does not have punctuation. Does the Old Tongue?]]The Old Tongue does not describe any rules for punctuation such as the period/full stop, question mark, colon etc. This is, however, not a necessary featue of a language. Classical Latin and Greek employed neither punctuation not spaces between words - known as [[wikipedia:scriptio continua|scriptio continua]]. It is presumed that the Old Tongue did place spaces between words. One other practice used in Latin was to write each sentence on a new line.

Several languages did not use any punctuaion until modern times eg.Thai, Chinese, Arabic, Persian, Urdu and Japanese. Although it seems a useful feature for a complex language such as the Old Tongue to use, we cannot assume it to be true.
